titre: The Tool That Rewrites Life Comes From a Yogurt Problem
accroche: CRISPR was discovered by industrial researchers looking for virus-resistant bacteria in starter cultures
contenu_vulgarise:
Making yogurt requires living bacteria. These bacteria have viruses, the bacteriophages, and a contamination can ruin an entire production run. It is an ordinary industrial problem, costly, and as old as fermentation.

In the 2000s, a Danish starter-culture company sets out to select naturally resistant strains. Its researchers compare the genomes of bacteria that survive attacks with those that do not.

## What they find in the genome

Certain regions of the bacterial genome had intrigued people since the 1980s without anyone knowing what they were for: short sequences, repeated at regular intervals, separated by variable segments. They were called CRISPR, after their description.

In 2005, the team notices that these variable segments resemble virus DNA.

The reading that then imposes itself is spectacular in its simplicity. These regions are an archive: when a bacterium survives an attack, it files a fragment of the virus in its genome. This fragment then serves as a recognition template; an associated protein compares it with incoming DNA, and cuts if it matches.

A bacterium thus possesses an immune memory, heritable, from which the history of infections can be read.

The 2007 paper demonstrates it experimentally. Since 2011, industrial starter cultures have been selected on this basis.

## From natural system to tool

What follows rests on the fact that a recognition mechanism is an addressing mechanism.

If the protein cuts the DNA that matches the archived fragment, then changing the fragment changes the target. One can therefore supply it with a guide of one's choosing and make it cut a precise sequence, in any genome.

This reformulation earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and turned genome editing into a routine laboratory operation.

## What the story teaches

CRISPR is readily cited as an argument for basic research. That is not quite accurate, and the case is more interesting than that.

The repeated sequences were described out of curiosity, with no use in sight, which is indeed basic research. But their function was elucidated by industrial researchers working on a very applied problem: saving vats of yogurt.

Neither alone would have been enough. Those who had the object did not have the question; those who had the question were not looking for that object.

And no one, in either team, was working on rewriting the human genome.

carte.punch: The tool that rewrites life comes from a yogurt-vat problem.
carte.idee: CRISPR regions had intrigued people since the 1980s. Their function was elucidated by starter-culture industry researchers looking for virus-resistant bacteria: it is an archive of past infections, hence an addressing system.

quiz.question: What are the variable segments of bacterial CRISPR regions?
choix: Fragments of virus DNA, archived after a survived infection
Copying errors accumulated over cell divisions
Resistance genes exchanged between neighboring bacteria
Regulatory sequences that control the rate of reproduction
quiz.explication: A bacterium that survives an attack files a fragment of the virus in its genome: the CRISPR region is an archive of past infections, readable like a history. This fragment then serves as a recognition template, and it is this addressing mechanism that was repurposed to cut any chosen sequence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What industrial problem led to the elucidation of the function of CRISPR regions?
choix: The rising cost of the milk used in making starter cultures
The viruses that infect bacteria and ruin an entire production run
The difficulty of keeping yogurts beyond a few weeks
The appearance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in the vats
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A Danish starter-culture company was looking for strains naturally resistant to bacteriophages, whose contamination can ruin an entire production run. Its researchers compared the genomes of bacteria that survive attacks with those that do not.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What makes it possible to turn this bacterial system into an editing tool?
choix: The fact that the protein cuts at random, which multiplies the attempts
The fact that the bacterium passes its cuts on to its descendants
The fact that changing the archived fragment changes the sequence that is cut
The fact that the repeated sequences copy themselves from one genome to another
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A recognition mechanism is an addressing mechanism: if the protein cuts the DNA that matches the archived fragment, then supplying it with a guide of one's choosing amounts to designating the target, in any genome.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the entry conclude about the role of basic research in this story?
choix: It did everything, industry having merely funded the work
It described the sequences, industry found their function
It played no role, everything having come from the fermentation vats
It aimed, as early as the 1980s, at rewriting the human genome
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The repeated sequences were indeed described out of curiosity, with no use in sight. But their function was elucidated by industrial researchers on a very applied problem, saving vats of yogurt: those who had the object did not have the question.
